forces: Concert band; arrangement by Lawrence Odom
performers: United States Air Force Band, Concert Band
intro: The United States Air Force Band plays Lawrence Odom’s arrangement of the Waltz of the Flowers. Long, singing melodies ride above a three-beat dance, dressed here in brass and woodwind.

relations.label: The principal waltz returns
relations.basis: The principal D-major waltz returns after the contrasting dance melodies. The first excerpt comes from its earlier restatement, and the later excerpt lies in the return marked near 302 s; both belong to the same principal group in Odom’s band arrangement. CENS diagonal mean 0.938, sustained 55 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 148.5 s (cache/form/tchaikovsky-waltz-flowers.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A band at Christmas
cues.text: The United States Air Force Band records this waltz for its 1996 album Christmas on Stage and Screen. Lawrence Odom’s arrangement brings Tchaikovsky’s ballet orchestra into the band’s brass-and-woodwind sound.
cues.evidence: The recording’s source credits Lawrence Odom and identifies track 6 of Christmas on Stage and Screen (1996). https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Waltz_of_the_Flowers_-_Concert_Band_-_United_States_Air_Force_Band.mp3

cues.title: Broken chords before the dance
cues.text: The cadenza runs up and down through broken chords, delaying the regular waltz. Tchaikovsky writes ad libitum over the solo: the player has room to linger before the final chords come to rest.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson orchestral score, plate 17668, pp. 4–5: harp cadenza marked ad libitum, ending with held chords. The recording uses Lawrence Odom’s band arrangement. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three beats beneath the tune
cues.text: The waltz begins in D major. A low first beat and two answering chords keep the dance moving while the melody stretches across the bar lines. Shorter, curling phrases answer the long tune.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, pp. 5–6: D-major waltz accompaniment, horn melody and clarinet replies. This note describes the melody and accompaniment retained in the band version. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two masterpieces, given time
cues.text: In Rouen in April 1891, Tchaikovsky asks Ivan Vsevolozhsky to postpone The Nutcracker and Iolanta. With enough time, he promises “two masterpieces (pardon my immodesty)”. His ship for America leaves in two days, and the ballet is still unfinished.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Ivan Vsevolozhsky, letter 4363, Rouen, 3/15 April 1891. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=The_Nutcracker

cues.title: A high tune, a low answer
cues.text: A high, lightly stepping melody opens the middle of the waltz. A longer tune follows lower down in B minor. The bass and offbeat chords keep their three-beat pattern beneath both.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, pp. 14–17, rehearsal letters E–F: upper-wind tune followed by the B-minor viola-and-cello melody. The description follows the tunes, without assigning the original string parts to Odom’s band. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The concert before the ballet
cues.text: Tchaikovsky conducts the suite in Saint Petersburg on 19 March 1892, nine months before the ballet reaches the stage. The waltz comes last. Two days later he tells his publisher: “The suite from the ballet was successful.”
cues.evidence: Suite première 7/19 March 1892; Tchaikovsky to Pyotr Jurgenson, letter 4641, 9/21 March 1892. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/The_Nutcracker_(suite)

cues.title: The familiar waltz returns
cues.text: The principal waltz melodies return in D major. This time the dance is already under way: the three-beat accompaniment carries the music straight into the returning phrases, with no second cadenza.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, p. 20 onwards, rehearsal H: return of the principal waltz group in D major. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: D major closes the suite
cues.text: Repeated chords bring the waltz to its emphatic D-major close. In the concert suite, this is the end of the evening. In the theatre, the dancers still have the pas de deux ahead of them.
cues.evidence: Final D-major chords: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, p. 35, https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624. Movement orders: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/The_Nutcracker_(suite) and https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=The_Nutcracker.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The chords release a cadenza
transitions.how: The introduction settles on A, the dominant of D major. Sustained ensemble chords give way to exposed broken chords, marked ad libitum in the score. The cadenza lets the soloist range freely across the notes before the waltz finds its steady three beats.
transitions.evidence: Jurgenson orchestral score, plate 17668, pp. 3–5. The solo is originally for harp; this recording is Lawrence Odom’s concert-band arrangement. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624

transitions.title: The bass starts the waltz
transitions.how: The cadenza ends with held dominant chords. D major arrives with a regular bass note on the first beat and chords on the next two. The long principal melody begins above this accompaniment; the free solo has become a measured dance.
transitions.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, p. 5: held cadenza chords, a tempo accompaniment, then the D-major horn theme. Melodic and harmonic description for the band arrangement. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624

transitions.title: A lighter tune keeps the dance moving
transitions.to: B · High melody and minor-key answer
transitions.how: The principal group gives way to a high, lightly articulated tune in D major. The bass and offbeat chords continue underneath. A lower, more sustained melody follows in B minor, with rising runs above it.
transitions.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, pp. 14–17, rehearsal E–F. The original upper-wind and lower-string tunes provide the melodic outline for this band-version note. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624

transitions.title: D major brings the waltz back
transitions.from: B · High melody and minor-key answer
transitions.how: A descending bass line leads into the return of the principal waltz group in D major. The accompaniment keeps moving in three, and the familiar melody enters without the introductory cadenza. The score marks the returning tune cantabile.
transitions.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, p. 20, rehearsal H: descending bass link, D-major return and cantabile marking. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624

composer.epithet: He could make a ballroom glitter, then let one unguarded melody tell us who was unhappy there.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas arrived in the middle of conversations; he held them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper that came to hand. Waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. Then he broke off for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, moving on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form. Here is the composer of extravagant passions in his own voice: observant, companionable, exact about his trade.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while opera and concerts increasingly claimed his attention.
